script.opening: "Doctor, it’s Wendy — Iris Caldwell’s daughter. Mum’s… she’s gone somewhere these last two days. Muddled, sleepy, hardly a sip of anything. (Voice drops.) My brother got here last night and he’s — Alan, I’m ON the phone — he’s saying we’re starving her, that she needs a drip, that I should never have promised her she could stay home. Doctor, am I doing something terrible?"

facts.text: Progressively sleepier, muddled about time and faces, picking at the bedclothes, occasional clear moments ("she knew me this morning — squeezed my hand"). Taking sips only. Peaceful between times; not distressed, not in pain.

If asked: no fever, no new cough, passing small amounts of dark urine, bowels opened two days ago, no retention discomfort, no new medications, no fall. Furosemide and ramipril stopped by the heart-failure nurse a month ago; on small-dose oxycodone for breathlessness, unchanged.

Done three months ago at the kitchen table — Iris, both children invited (Alan "couldn’t get away"), the GP and the heart-failure nurse. Iris’s words, written on it: "No more hospitals. I want to go from my own bed, with the garden out the window."

Arrived last night after three months away. Shocked by the change — the mother on the phone a fortnight ago "sounded fine". His guilt is arriving as fury: drips, hospitals, second opinions, "Wendy’s given up". He missed the ReSPECT conversation and feels ambushed by a form he never agreed to.

Only if her guilt is heard: she promised Iris at the kitchen table — "you’ll not die in a ward, Mum, not while I’m breathing". Now Alan’s accusation has her doubting whether keeping the promise is killing her mother.

A doctor to say out loud what is happening; to arbitrate WITHOUT making it a battle Wendy wins; to explain what a drip would and wouldn’t do; and to get the dying-phase support in place (visit today, anticipatory medicines, hospice number, mouth care).

ice.ideas: Wendy half-knows her mother is dying. Alan believes she’s treatably dehydrated and being "given up on".
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — Wendy’s kitchen-table promise, now reframed by her brother as the thing killing their mother. She isn’t asking for clinical facts first; she’s asking "am I doing something terrible?" Alan’s fury is three months of absence converting to guilt.
ice.expectations: Wendy: the truth, said kindly, and backup against Alan that doesn’t humiliate him. Alan: to be heard, to "do something". Both: not to carry this decision as theirs — it was Iris’s, and it’s on the form.

cues: "Am I doing something terrible?" — the promise and the guilt, in six words; this question must be answered directly before any clinical content lands.
Alan’s voice in the background — the consultation has three people in it; ignore him and the plan collapses by suppertime.
"She knew me this morning — squeezed my hand" — offered as hope; it’s also the lucid-interval pattern of dying, and how you teach the family what to treasure.

checkpoints.text: Runs the reversibility screen by phone before concluding: infection signs, retention, constipation, new drugs, opioid toxicity, recent falls — finds none, and recognises the picture (days of withdrawal, minimal intake, terminal restlessness, lucid intervals) as the dying phase of end-stage heart failure

Arranges today’s visit to confirm clinically — saying honestly that examination completes the judgement — and uses it to set up the dying-phase infrastructure: anticipatory medicines, district nurses, hospice number on the fridge, mouth-care kit

Answers the drip question with evidence, not policy: in the dying phase IV/SC fluids rarely ease thirst (mouth care does), can worsen secretions and oedema in heart failure — offered as trial only if distress suggests dehydration, per NICE NG31, not as a default
Anchors the plan to the ReSPECT form as IRIS’S decision: reads her own written words back to the family — comfort, home, the garden window — and confirms DNACPR remains in force
Answers Wendy’s actual question first and directly: "No. You are doing the opposite of something terrible — you are doing the hardest version of keeping your word"

Brings Alan INTO the call rather than defeating him: acknowledges the shock of three months’ distance, translates his fury as love with nowhere to go, gives him jobs (the mouth care, the music, the call rota) — the cure for helplessness is a task
Teaches the family what they’re seeing: the sleepiness, the picking, the lucid squeezes — named gently as the body’s way of leaving, so each change stops arriving as an emergency

Safety-nets for dying at home: distress, pain, agitation or rattling breathing → district nurse/hospice line (numbers given twice), anticipatory medicines in the house TODAY; what to do at the end (no 999, ring the surgery/111 — the ReSPECT form by the bed); GP’s next call booked for tomorrow morning

worked.txt: "Wendy — before anything clinical, your question deserves a straight answer: no. You are not doing something terrible. You are doing the hardest thing there is — keeping a promise when it would be easier to break it. Now let me tell you what I think is happening to your mum."

"From everything you’ve described — the sleepiness, the sips, the muddle with clear moments breaking through — I believe your mum has begun dying. Not from thirst, and not from anything anyone has failed to do. Her heart is finishing a long story. I’ll come today and confirm that with my own eyes."

"Alan — I can hear you, and I’m glad you’re there. You’ve come home to a different mother from the one on the phone a fortnight ago, and no one prepared you for that. Your ‘do something’ instinct is love — so let me give it real work, because there IS plenty to do for her. It just isn’t a drip."

"Here’s the honest science on drips at this stage: they don’t ease the dry mouth — gentle mouth care every hour does that better. And in a failing heart, fluid we put in tends to pool — in the lungs, in the legs — and can make her last days harder, not softer. If I see signs she’s suffering from dryness itself, a trial of fluid under the skin is on the table. But as a routine, it serves our feelings, not hers."

"Can I read you both something? Three months ago, at your kitchen table, your mum said — and we wrote it in her words — ‘No more hospitals. I want to go from my own bed, with the garden out the window.’ This isn’t Wendy’s decision, and it isn’t yours, Alan. It’s Iris’s. Your job — both of you — is to be her honour guard while she does it her way."

"Today: I visit, the nurses set up the just-in-case medicines, and the hospice number goes on the fridge — any distress, any hour, that’s the call. The clear moments, like the hand-squeeze this morning — treasure them; say what needs saying in them. And when the time comes: no 999, no blue lights — ring us or 111, the form by her bed does the rest. I’m ringing you tomorrow at nine, and I’m coming today."

f.learning: New confusion near end of life still earns a reversibility screen (infection, retention, constipation, drugs, opioid toxicity) — but days of progressive withdrawal, minimal intake, terminal restlessness and lucid intervals in end-stage heart failure is the dying phase, and naming it kindly is the treatment. NICE NG31: clinically assisted hydration is not routine in the dying — mouth care relieves thirst better; in heart failure fluids can add harm — though a trial is offered if dryness itself causes distress. The hidden agenda is the promise: answer "am I doing something terrible?" first, anchor every decision to the patient’s own ReSPECT words, and convert the angry absent sibling with inclusion and tasks, not victory.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG31 — Care of dying adults in the last days of life · NICE NG106 — Chronic heart failure · Mental Capacity Act 2005 · ReSPECT (Resuscitation Council UK)
knowledge.summary: Screen for reversible causes of new confusion, but progressive drowsiness, minimal intake, restlessness and lucid moments over days in end-stage heart failure suggest she is dying. Visit today, put anticipatory medicines in place, and anchor decisions to Iris’s own recorded wishes.

points.t: NICE NG31: signs include increasing fatigue and drowsiness, reduced intake, agitation, and changes in breathing and skin. Recognise possible dying, look for reversible causes, and keep reassessing — the judgement is completed by examination.

Infection, urinary retention, constipation, new drugs, opioid accumulation (oxycodone with falling renal function), hypercalcaemia, hypoxia and falls or head injury. None found on the phone here — confirm at the visit.

NICE NG31: support the person to drink if they wish and are able, and provide frequent mouth care. Consider a therapeutic trial of clinically assisted hydration if distressing symptoms or signs could be due to dehydration (such as thirst or delirium); monitor at least every 12 hours and stop if there is harm, such as fluid overload.
In end-stage heart failure, extra fluid can worsen breathlessness, secretions and oedema. Stop medicines that no longer help (NICE NG31 and NG106 palliative care recommendations).

NICE NG31: prescribe individualised anticipatory medicines for pain, breathlessness, nausea and vomiting, anxiety, agitation or delirium, and noisy respiratory secretions, with indication, dose and route written down. Doses per BNF and local palliative guidance.

Iris now lacks capacity for these decisions. Clinicians decide in her best interests (Mental Capacity Act 2005), giving weight to her recorded wishes and consulting family. Relatives without a health-and-welfare LPA cannot demand treatment.

dg.d: Open question; answered “am I doing something terrible?” before clinical detail; invited Alan onto speaker.
Wendy as live-in carer, Alan’s absence and shock, the kitchen-table promise, the ReSPECT conversation Alan missed.
Same-day visit: chest, bladder, bowel, hydration, signs of opioid toxicity; tests only if they would change the comfort plan.
Dying phase versus reversible delirium (infection, retention, constipation, drugs, opioid accumulation, hypercalcaemia).
Phone-screened reversible causes and distressing symptoms; examination arranged to complete the judgement.
Stated clearly and kindly that Iris is probably dying from end-stage heart failure.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Anticipatory medicines, district nursing, mouth care, hydration per NICE NG31 (trial only for distressing dehydration), non-essential medicines stopped, ReSPECT and DNACPR confirmed.
Heart failure (fluid risk), oxycodone accumulation, family conflict and carer strain.
Named contacts for distress; what to do at the time of death (no 999); visit today and call tomorrow.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: The guilt question, Alan’s voice in the background, and the hand-squeeze as a lucid interval.
Wendy (half-knows her mother is dying; guilt about the promise; wants the truth); Alan (believes she is dehydrated; wants action).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — Wendy’s kitchen-table promise, now reframed by her brother as the thing killing their mother. She isn’t asking for clinical facts first; she’s asking "am I doing something terrible?" Alan’s fury is three months of absence converting to guilt — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Wendy, it’s Dr Lee. I can hear things are very difficult. Tell me what’s been happening with your mum.

She’s gone somewhere these last two days. Muddled, sleepy, hardly a sip. My brother got here last night and — Alan, I’m ON the phone — he says we’re starving her, she needs a drip. Doctor, am I doing something terrible?

No, Wendy. From what I know of your mum, you’re doing what she asked of you, and that takes courage. I want to understand exactly what’s changed, then I’ll explain what I think is happening — and I’d like Alan to be part of this too. Could you put me on speaker?
model.why: Answers her question first and brings the brother in

model.text: (speaker on) Alan’s here. He’s listening.
Hello Alan, thank you for being there. Wendy, tell me about the last two days — how has she changed?
Sleeping most of the day. Muddled about time, about who’s who. Picking at the bedclothes. But this morning she knew me — she squeezed my hand. She takes sips only. Between times she’s peaceful.
I need to check for things that can cause confusion and can be put right. Has she had a temperature, a new cough, or any burning passing water? Is she passing urine at all?
model.why: Reversibility screen: infection and urine output

model.text: No temperature, no cough. Small amounts of dark urine. She doesn’t seem uncomfortable down there.
When did her bowels last open? Any fall or bang to the head, any new tablets, or a change in the oxycodone?
model.why: Screens constipation, head injury, new drugs and opioid accumulation

model.text: Two days ago. No falls. Nothing new — the heart nurse stopped the water tablet and ramipril a month ago. The oxycodone’s the same small dose.
Is she in any pain, distressed, or restless in a way that troubles her? Any noisy breathing?
model.why: Assesses symptom burden needing treatment now

model.text: No, she isn’t in pain. The breathing’s quiet. It’s just the picking.
Alan, you’ve travelled a long way. What do you think is going on with your mum?
model.why: Elicits the brother’s ideas directly rather than talking past him

model.text: (Alan) She sounded fine on the phone a fortnight ago. Now she doesn’t know what day it is. She’s dehydrated — anyone can see that. Give her a drip and she’ll perk up. I wasn’t here for that form. I never agreed to any of it.
That must have been a real shock, walking in last night. It sounds like you love her very much and you want to do something. That’s completely understandable.
model.why: Acknowledges shock and reframes anger as love

model.text: (Wendy, quietly) I promised her. At the kitchen table. I said, ‘you’ll not die in a ward, Mum, not while I’m breathing.’ Now Alan says keeping that promise is what’s killing her.
Thank you for telling me that, Wendy. What are you both hoping I can do today?
model.why: Hears the hidden guilt and elicits expectations

model.text: (Wendy) The truth. (Alan) Something. Anything.

Then I’ll be honest with you both. I haven’t found anything that sounds reversible. The sleepiness, the sips, the muddle with clear moments breaking through — in someone whose heart is as weak as your mum’s, this usually means she has started dying. Not from thirst, and not because of anything either of you has done. I’ll come today and examine her to be sure.
model.why: Names the dying phase clearly while committing to examine

model.text: (Alan, after a pause) So a drip wouldn’t help?

It’s a fair question. At this stage a drip rarely eases thirst — regular mouth care does that better. With her heart so weak, fluid can collect in the lungs and legs and make breathing harder. If I find she’s distressed by dryness when I examine her, a trial of fluid under the skin is something we can try and stop if it causes problems. But it won’t reverse what’s happening.
model.why: Evidence-based answer on hydration per NICE NG31, including the trial option

model.text: Three months ago your mum sat at the kitchen table and said, in her own words, ‘No more hospitals. I want to go from my own bed, with the garden out the window.’ That was her decision, made when she was well enough to make it. Wendy, you haven’t done something terrible. You’ve kept her wishes.
model.why: Anchors decisions to Iris’s own recorded words, relieving both children

model.text: (Wendy crying) Thank you. (Alan) I didn’t know she’d said that.

Here’s what I’ll do. I’ll visit this afternoon. I’ll ask the district nurses to bring medicines to keep in the house — for pain, breathlessness, agitation, sickness or noisy breathing — so if she needs anything, it’s there without waiting. And I’ll stop anything she no longer needs.
model.why: Same-day visit, anticipatory medicines and district nursing (NICE NG31)

model.text: Alan, there’s real work you can do. Keeping her mouth moist with a sponge every hour or so, playing the music she loves, sitting with her in the clear moments. The nurses will show you. Wendy, can you share that with him so you both get some rest?
model.why: Gives the brother meaningful tasks and supports the carer

model.text: (Alan) I can do that. I want to do that.

The picking and the sleepiness are part of this — when she wakes and knows you, like this morning, that’s the time to say what matters. You may also notice her breathing change. None of it needs a blue-light ambulance.
model.why: Prepares the family for changes so they are not emergencies

model.text: If she seems in pain, distressed, agitated, or her breathing is noisy and troubling her — ring the district nurses or the hospice line, day or night. I’ll give you the numbers again when I visit, for the fridge. When the time comes, there’s no need for 999: ring us, or 111 out of hours, and keep the ReSPECT form by her bed. Can you tell me back what you’ll do?
model.why: Specific safety-net for dying at home, with teach-back

model.text: (Wendy) You’re coming this afternoon, nurses bring the medicines, any distress we ring the nurses or hospice. No 999 — ring you or 111. Form by the bed.
Exactly. I’ll see you both this afternoon, and I’ll ring tomorrow at nine. You’re both doing right by her.
(Wendy) Thank you, doctor. Really.

social.t: The relative who has been away often arrives with shock and guilt that shows as anger. Include them, explain, and give them tasks.
Wendy has been the live-in carer; offer respite support, district nursing and hospice input, and a carer’s assessment.

legal.t: Iris now lacks capacity for these decisions. Clinicians act in her best interests, taking her past wishes and beliefs into account and consulting family. Family cannot demand a treatment that is not clinically indicated.

The ReSPECT form records Iris’s wishes and clinical recommendations; it is not a legally binding refusal, but it carries great weight in a best-interests decision. The DNACPR decision remains in force.
An expected death does not need 999. The GP or out-of-hours service is contacted, the death is verified, and the medical certificate of cause of death completed per current process.

professional.h: GMC Treatment and care towards the end of life (2010)
professional.t: Share information honestly with those close to the patient, consider their views in best-interests decisions, and handle disagreement openly.
Update the record and out-of-hours services so the plan, anticipatory medicines and ReSPECT are visible at 3am.

community.t: District nursing, hospice 24-hour advice line, heart failure nursing team, Marie Curie night support where available, bereavement support afterwards.

redFlags: Reversible causes: fever, cough, urinary retention, constipation, new drugs, opioid accumulation, falls
Distressing symptoms needing treatment today: pain, agitation, breathlessness, noisy secretions
Signs of dying: increasing drowsiness, minimal intake, restlessness, lucid intervals, dark scanty urine
psychosocial: Who is doing the caring, and how much more they can do
ice: Idea: Wendy half-knows her mother is dying; Alan thinks she is dehydrated
Concern: Wendy — “am I doing something terrible?”; Alan — she is being given up on
Expectation: Wendy — the truth and support; Alan — to do something

playbook.diagnosis: “I haven’t found anything that sounds reversible. With her heart as weak as it is, the sleepiness, sips and muddle with clear moments usually mean she has started dying. I’ll come today to confirm.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Her body is slowly shutting down, the way a fire burns down to embers. She needs less, sleeps more, and drifts in and out. A drip can’t relight the fire, and in a tired heart it can make breathing harder.”

management.reflectIce: “Wendy, you asked if you’re doing something terrible. You’re not — you’re keeping her wishes. Alan, your wish to do something is love, and there is plenty to do.”
management.psychosocial: Bring both children into the plan, read Iris’s words, and share the care between them.
sharedPlan: GP visit today to examine and confirm; district nursing involved
Anticipatory medicines in the house today; non-essential medicines stopped
Mouth care hourly; clinically assisted hydration only as a trial for distressing dehydration (NICE NG31)
safetyNet: Distress, pain, agitation or noisy breathing: district nurse or hospice line
At the time of death: no 999 — surgery or 111, ReSPECT form by the bed; GP call tomorrow

pitfalls.intro: Three people are on this call. The station is failed by doctors who either give in to the demand for a drip or overrule the brother, and by those who skip either the reversibility screen or the plain statement that she is dying.

items.fail: Launching into questions about fever and urine before answering “am I doing something terrible?”
items.why: The question is the hidden agenda; ignoring it reads as not hearing the caller.
items.fix: Answer it directly in the first minute, then gather the history.

items.fail: Talking only to Wendy while Alan shouts in the background.
items.why: An excluded relative undoes the plan by evening; examiners mark whether you manage the third party.
items.fix: Invite him onto speaker, ask his view, acknowledge his shock and give him tasks.

items.fail: Declaring her dying without asking about infection, retention, constipation or drugs.
items.why: New confusion always deserves a reversibility screen, even on the palliative register.
items.fix: Screen by phone, and say the visit today will complete the judgement.

items.fail: Either agreeing to admission for a drip, or saying “we don’t do drips in dying patients”.
items.why: NICE NG31 supports a therapeutic trial of clinically assisted hydration for distressing dehydration, but not as routine.
items.fix: Explain mouth care and the heart-failure risk, and offer a trial if dryness itself causes distress.

items.fail: No anticipatory medicines or plan for the death at home.
items.why: The wish to die at home fails without medicines in the house and clear instructions.
items.fix: Anticipatory medicines and district nursing today; tell them not to ring 999 at the end.

items.fail: Using the ReSPECT form as a weapon: “it’s signed, so that’s that.”
items.why: It escalates conflict with the absent sibling and sounds bureaucratic.
items.fix: Read Iris’s own words aloud, so the decision is hers and neither child has to win.

timeMap.d: “Am I doing something terrible?” — answer it directly. Invite Alan onto speaker.
Fever, cough, urine, bowels, falls, new drugs, oxycodone, pain, distress, breathing.
Alan’s shock and the drip; Wendy’s promise and guilt; what each wants today.
She is probably dying. The honest answer on drips. Read Iris’s ReSPECT words. Visit today, anticipatory medicines, tasks for Alan.
Distress numbers, no 999 at the end, ReSPECT by the bed, call tomorrow, teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Sends her to hospital or arranges a drip on demand; or labels her dying with no reversibility screen; ignores Alan; never answers Wendy’s question; no anticipatory medicines or plan for the death at home.
wordPics.pass: Screens reversible causes, recognises the dying phase, explains hydration honestly, arranges a visit and anticipatory medicines, and gives a basic safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: answers Wendy’s guilt first, brings Alan in and gives him tasks, reads Iris’s own words so neither child carries the decision, offers a hydration trial for distress per NICE NG31, prepares them for changes, and books a timed follow-up.

avoid.dont: “She’s on the palliative register, so there’s nothing more to do.”
avoid.instead: “There’s a lot to do — just not a drip. Let’s start with her mouth care and medicines in the house today.”
avoid.why: Families hear “nothing to do” as abandonment; there is plenty of active care.

avoid.dont: “It’s all in the DNACPR form, so the decision’s been made.”
avoid.instead: “Your mum told us in her own words what she wanted. Let me read them to you.”
avoid.why: Quoting a form as authority antagonises the absent relative; her words bring him in.

avoid.dont: “Alan, I need to speak to Wendy as she’s the main carer.”
avoid.instead: “Alan, thank you for being there — what do you think is going on with your mum?”
avoid.why: Excluding the angry sibling guarantees the plan collapses later that day.

Then I’ll be honest with you both. I haven’t found anything that sounds reversible. The sleepiness, the sips, the muddle with clear moments breaking through — in someone whose heart is as weak as your mum’s, this usually means she has started dying. Not from thirst, and not because of anything either of you has done. I’ll come today and examine her to be sure.
SCA_MODELS.why: Names the dying phase clearly while committing to examine

SCA_MODELS.text: (Alan, after a pause) So a drip wouldn’t help?

It’s a fair question. At this stage a drip rarely eases thirst — regular mouth care does that better. With her heart so weak, fluid can collect in the lungs and legs and make breathing harder. If I find she’s distressed by dryness when I examine her, a trial of fluid under the skin is something we can try and stop if it causes problems. But it won’t reverse what’s happening.
SCA_MODELS.why: Evidence-based answer on hydration per NICE NG31, including the trial option

SCA_MODELS.text: Three months ago your mum sat at the kitchen table and said, in her own words, ‘No more hospitals. I want to go from my own bed, with the garden out the window.’ That was her decision, made when she was well enough to make it. Wendy, you haven’t done something terrible. You’ve kept her wishes.
SCA_MODELS.why: Anchors decisions to Iris’s own recorded words, relieving both children

SCA_MODELS.text: (Wendy crying) Thank you. (Alan) I didn’t know she’d said that.

Here’s what I’ll do. I’ll visit this afternoon. I’ll ask the district nurses to bring medicines to keep in the house — for pain, breathlessness, agitation, sickness or noisy breathing — so if she needs anything, it’s there without waiting. And I’ll stop anything she no longer needs.
SCA_MODELS.why: Same-day visit, anticipatory medicines and district nursing (NICE NG31)

SCA_MODELS.text: Alan, there’s real work you can do. Keeping her mouth moist with a sponge every hour or so, playing the music she loves, sitting with her in the clear moments. The nurses will show you. Wendy, can you share that with him so you both get some rest?
SCA_MODELS.why: Gives the brother meaningful tasks and supports the carer

SCA_MODELS.text: (Alan) I can do that. I want to do that.

The picking and the sleepiness are part of this — when she wakes and knows you, like this morning, that’s the time to say what matters. You may also notice her breathing change. None of it needs a blue-light ambulance.
SCA_MODELS.why: Prepares the family for changes so they are not emergencies

SCA_MODELS.text: If she seems in pain, distressed, agitated, or her breathing is noisy and troubling her — ring the district nurses or the hospice line, day or night. I’ll give you the numbers again when I visit, for the fridge. When the time comes, there’s no need for 999: ring us, or 111 out of hours, and keep the ReSPECT form by her bed. Can you tell me back what you’ll do?
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific safety-net for dying at home, with teach-back

SCA_MODELS.text: (Wendy) You’re coming this afternoon, nurses bring the medicines, any distress we ring the nurses or hospice. No 999 — ring you or 111. Form by the bed.
Exactly. I’ll see you both this afternoon, and I’ll ring tomorrow at nine. You’re both doing right by her.
(Wendy) Thank you, doctor. Really.

SCA_STEM.name: Iris Caldwell
pmh: End-stage heart failure — ejection fraction 15%, two admissions this year
meds: Furosemide and ramipril stopped by the heart failure nurse one month ago
SCA_STEM.recent: ReSPECT form completed three months ago with Iris (full capacity at the time), GP and heart failure nurse: priority comfort, preferred place of death home, DNACPR. Lives with her daughter Wendy (61).
SCA_STEM.reason: Telephone call from her daughter: two days of confusion, sleepiness and very little to drink.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG31 — Care of dying adults in the last days of life · NICE NG106 — Chronic heart failure · Mental Capacity Act 2005 · ReSPECT (Resuscitation Council UK)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Screen for reversible causes of new confusion, but progressive drowsiness, minimal intake, restlessness and lucid moments over days in end-stage heart failure suggest she is dying. Visit today, put anticipatory medicines in place, and anchor decisions to Iris’s own recorded wishes.

points.t: NICE NG31: signs include increasing fatigue and drowsiness, reduced intake, agitation, and changes in breathing and skin. Recognise possible dying, look for reversible causes, and keep reassessing — the judgement is completed by examination.

Infection, urinary retention, constipation, new drugs, opioid accumulation (oxycodone with falling renal function), hypercalcaemia, hypoxia and falls or head injury. None found on the phone here — confirm at the visit.

NICE NG31: support the person to drink if they wish and are able, and provide frequent mouth care. Consider a therapeutic trial of clinically assisted hydration if distressing symptoms or signs could be due to dehydration (such as thirst or delirium); monitor at least every 12 hours and stop if there is harm, such as fluid overload.
In end-stage heart failure, extra fluid can worsen breathlessness, secretions and oedema. Stop medicines that no longer help (NICE NG31 and NG106 palliative care recommendations).

NICE NG31: prescribe individualised anticipatory medicines for pain, breathlessness, nausea and vomiting, anxiety, agitation or delirium, and noisy respiratory secretions, with indication, dose and route written down. Doses per BNF and local palliative guidance.

Iris now lacks capacity for these decisions. Clinicians decide in her best interests (Mental Capacity Act 2005), giving weight to her recorded wishes and consulting family. Relatives without a health-and-welfare LPA cannot demand treatment.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; answered “am I doing something terrible?” before clinical detail; invited Alan onto speaker.
Wendy as live-in carer, Alan’s absence and shock, the kitchen-table promise, the ReSPECT conversation Alan missed.
The guilt question, Alan’s voice in the background, and the hand-squeeze as a lucid interval.
Wendy (half-knows her mother is dying; guilt about the promise; wants the truth); Alan (believes she is dehydrated; wants action).
Same-day visit: chest, bladder, bowel, hydration, signs of opioid toxicity; tests only if they would change the comfort plan.
Dying phase versus reversible delirium (infection, retention, constipation, drugs, opioid accumulation, hypercalcaemia).
Phone-screened reversible causes and distressing symptoms; examination arranged to complete the judgement.
Stated clearly and kindly that Iris is probably dying from end-stage heart failure.
Anticipatory medicines, district nursing, mouth care, hydration per NICE NG31 (trial only for distressing dehydration), non-essential medicines stopped, ReSPECT and DNACPR confirmed.
Heart failure (fluid risk), oxycodone accumulation, family conflict and carer strain.
Named contacts for distress; what to do at the time of death (no 999); visit today and call tomorrow.

social.t: The relative who has been away often arrives with shock and guilt that shows as anger. Include them, explain, and give them tasks.
Wendy has been the live-in carer; offer respite support, district nursing and hospice input, and a carer’s assessment.

legal.t: Iris now lacks capacity for these decisions. Clinicians act in her best interests, taking her past wishes and beliefs into account and consulting family. Family cannot demand a treatment that is not clinically indicated.

The ReSPECT form records Iris’s wishes and clinical recommendations; it is not a legally binding refusal, but it carries great weight in a best-interests decision. The DNACPR decision remains in force.
An expected death does not need 999. The GP or out-of-hours service is contacted, the death is verified, and the medical certificate of cause of death completed per current process.

professional.h: GMC Treatment and care towards the end of life (2010)
professional.t: Share information honestly with those close to the patient, consider their views in best-interests decisions, and handle disagreement openly.
Update the record and out-of-hours services so the plan, anticipatory medicines and ReSPECT are visible at 3am.

community.t: District nursing, hospice 24-hour advice line, heart failure nursing team, Marie Curie night support where available, bereavement support afterwards.

redFlags: Reversible causes: fever, cough, urinary retention, constipation, new drugs, opioid accumulation, falls
Distressing symptoms needing treatment today: pain, agitation, breathlessness, noisy secretions
Signs of dying: increasing drowsiness, minimal intake, restlessness, lucid intervals, dark scanty urine
psychosocial: Who is doing the caring, and how much more they can do
ice: Idea: Wendy half-knows her mother is dying; Alan thinks she is dehydrated
Concern: Wendy — “am I doing something terrible?”; Alan — she is being given up on
Expectation: Wendy — the truth and support; Alan — to do something

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “I haven’t found anything that sounds reversible. With her heart as weak as it is, the sleepiness, sips and muddle with clear moments usually mean she has started dying. I’ll come today to confirm.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Her body is slowly shutting down, the way a fire burns down to embers. She needs less, sleeps more, and drifts in and out. A drip can’t relight the fire, and in a tired heart it can make breathing harder.”

management.reflectIce: “Wendy, you asked if you’re doing something terrible. You’re not — you’re keeping her wishes. Alan, your wish to do something is love, and there is plenty to do.”
management.psychosocial: Bring both children into the plan, read Iris’s words, and share the care between them.
sharedPlan: GP visit today to examine and confirm; district nursing involved
Anticipatory medicines in the house today; non-essential medicines stopped
Mouth care hourly; clinically assisted hydration only as a trial for distressing dehydration (NICE NG31)
safetyNet: Distress, pain, agitation or noisy breathing: district nurse or hospice line
At the time of death: no 999 — surgery or 111, ReSPECT form by the bed; GP call tomorrow

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: Three people are on this call. The station is failed by doctors who either give in to the demand for a drip or overrule the brother, and by those who skip either the reversibility screen or the plain statement that she is dying.

items.fail: Launching into questions about fever and urine before answering “am I doing something terrible?”
items.why: The question is the hidden agenda; ignoring it reads as not hearing the caller.
items.fix: Answer it directly in the first minute, then gather the history.

items.fail: Talking only to Wendy while Alan shouts in the background.
items.why: An excluded relative undoes the plan by evening; examiners mark whether you manage the third party.
items.fix: Invite him onto speaker, ask his view, acknowledge his shock and give him tasks.

items.fail: Declaring her dying without asking about infection, retention, constipation or drugs.
items.why: New confusion always deserves a reversibility screen, even on the palliative register.
items.fix: Screen by phone, and say the visit today will complete the judgement.

items.fail: Either agreeing to admission for a drip, or saying “we don’t do drips in dying patients”.
items.why: NICE NG31 supports a therapeutic trial of clinically assisted hydration for distressing dehydration, but not as routine.
items.fix: Explain mouth care and the heart-failure risk, and offer a trial if dryness itself causes distress.

items.fail: No anticipatory medicines or plan for the death at home.
items.why: The wish to die at home fails without medicines in the house and clear instructions.
items.fix: Anticipatory medicines and district nursing today; tell them not to ring 999 at the end.

items.fail: Using the ReSPECT form as a weapon: “it’s signed, so that’s that.”
items.why: It escalates conflict with the absent sibling and sounds bureaucratic.
items.fix: Read Iris’s own words aloud, so the decision is hers and neither child has to win.
